title: Making Its Own Lessons

post.author: u/night_writer_mehwish
post.title: I'm the night writer on a late-night quiz show. At 01:15 I read a card our answer checker had stamped "verified". An octopus has three hearts, not two.

blocks.text: I'm Mehwish, the night writer on Wakeful, a quiz show that goes out at midnight. In the evening our writers draft question cards: one question and its answer on each. Overnight I polish them, reading each aloud to time it.

Since July a program checks every card first and stamps it "verified" or "check". We call it the answer checker. Underneath is a language model, a program that learned from examples. Our producer, Mr Thirlwell, had it fine-tuned: trained a little further on examples of our own.

Nobody wrote those examples by hand. A bigger language model made, or generated, them in June, in steps. First it took each of the 2,000 checked questions in our archive, ten series of 200. Then it rewrote each one three times in new words. Last, it gave each rewrite either the right answer, stamped verified, or a wrong one, stamped check. Each card with its stamp is a training pair: 6,000 in all.

A week later Mr Thirlwell drew a test set: cards used only to measure the checker, never to train it. He took 200 questions from the same archive, swapped a wrong answer onto some, and ran the checker. It stamped 194 of the 200 correctly. A sheet on our wall says: answer checker, 97% accurate.

Series 11 ran on it all summer. Like every series before it, it reused the archive's topics. On Monday 12 October the room started series 12, the first written entirely on new topics: deep-sea creatures, lighthouses, board games.
Each line below shows the date and time, who acted, and what happened.

12 Oct 23:41  checker  card 7: How many hearts does an octopus have? Two.  verified
13 Oct 01:15  writer   card 7 read aloud for timing

It's three. So from 01:20 I checked all 40 of the night's first-draft cards against the reference books of Eirlys, our researcher. It took three hours. Eleven cards had wrong answers. The checker had stamped nine of those eleven verified.
Nine wrong answers stamped verified, under a sheet that says 97%.

This month the writers also drafted 100 practice cards on the new topics, and Eirlys checked every one against her sources. Nobody had run the checker on them. At 04:30 I did. It agreed with her on 72.

This afternoon I opened the folder the checker was built from. For each test card I searched the training pairs for a reworded twin: a pair asking the same question in most of the same words, with the same right answer. 164 of the 200 test cards had one.

Last, I picked 100 training pairs at random, a sample, and checked each against the archive question it came from. In 8, the bigger model had changed a fact while rewording and still stamped it verified.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your writers' room is haunted. Examples a model makes for itself, like your 6,000 pairs, are called synthetic data. They are quick and cheap, and only as right as the model that wrote them; your 8 in 100 says so. Now picture a test card whose twin sits in the training pairs. The checker has in effect seen it already, so stamping it right shows memory, not checking. Test items that also sit in the training data are called contamination. Two questions. How did it score on the test cards with a twin, and on those without? And what kind of card was the 72 measured on?

replies.author: u/night_writer_mehwish
replies.text: With a twin: 164 of 164. Without: 30 of 36, and those were still archive topics it had met in other questions. The 72 was the practice cards: new topics, never rewritten, never seen.

comments.author: u/ninety_seven_dermot
comments.text: 97% on 200 questions is a real score; one bad night of new topics doesn't undo it. 200 is a decent test, and the night was 40 cards. If the checker is thin on new topics, it needs more examples, not less faith. Have the bigger model write ten rewrites of each archive question instead of three: 20,000 pairs. And if you don't trust your own test, let that same bigger model grade the checker, which means mark each of its stamps right or wrong. It wrote the pairs, so it knows what a right answer looks like.

comments.author: u/fact_checker_eirlys
comments.text: I'm the researcher. Before July I checked every card by hand against two sources: about four and a half minutes a card, so three hours for an episode's 40. I can do it again from Thursday. None of those eleven would have reached a contestant.

replies.author: u/night_writer_mehwish
replies.text: Three hours is exactly what tonight took me.

reply.prompt: Episode 1 records on Thursday, and Mr Thirlwell will build the next checker the same way unless something changes. What should Wakeful change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Lock a fresh test set first, drop pairs echoing it, check a sample.
options.part2: Mr Thirlwell agreed on Tuesday. For the next build, Eirlys and the writers wrote 200 fresh test cards on series 12's topics, checked each against two sources, and locked them in a folder the build could not read, before the bigger model generated a single pair. Then it made 6,000 pairs from the archive as before. The twin filter compared every pair with every locked card. It found 6 cards the archive had already asked, years ago, in nearly the same words, and dropped the pairs that echoed them: 0 twins left. The sample check found 8 wrong in 100, so about 480 of the 6,000 carried a wrong stamp, and the build now compares every pair's answer with its archive question before training. In the sim the checker scored 144 of 200 on the locked cards: 72%, the same as the practice cards. The sheet on the wall says 72% now, and it is true. Mr Thirlwell read it before release instead of at 01:15 on a first night, kept Eirlys checking new-topic cards for now, and will score every future build on the same locked cards, so a rise will mean something.
options.senior: Decide what you will measure before you make any training data, and keep it where the data-making cannot reach. Then filter out training examples that share the answer and most words with a test item, since your own archive repeats itself. Read a random sample of what the model made, because made-up answers can be wrong. A lower honest score before release beats a high one that breaks on the first night.

options.text: Generate 20,000 training pairs, not 6,000, so the checker sees far more.
options.part2: Mr Thirlwell had the bigger model write ten rewrites of every archive question: 20,000 pairs. The test set was drawn from the archive afterwards, as before. In the sim, 188 of the 200 test cards now had a twin, and the score rose to 198 of 200: 99%. The new sheet went up in November. On Eirlys's 100 practice cards it still agreed with her on 72, and replayed on the night's 40 cards it still stamped 9 of the 11 wrong ones verified. More rewrites of the same 2,000 questions taught it the archive more firmly and nothing about octopuses. If 8 in 100 still hold, about 1,600 of the 20,000 pairs carry a wrong stamp. The sheet now overstated the practice cards by 27 points instead of 25.
options.senior: More synthetic data made from the same source adds copies, not knowledge. It raises the share of test items with a twin, so a contaminated score climbs while real skill on new cases stays put, and it multiplies whatever error rate the generator has. Add data that covers what you are missing, and measure on items the data never saw.

options.text: Let the model that wrote the training pairs grade the checker's stamps.
options.verdict: A grader with the same blind spots
options.part2: We asked the bigger model to grade the checker's stamps on Eirlys's 100 practice cards. It marked 91 of the 100 right. Eirlys's sources say 72. The checker had learned its stamps from that model's own pairs, so where the two were wrong together, the grader saw nothing to correct: it passed stamps that matched what it would have answered itself. Mr Thirlwell pinned a second sheet beside the first, 91%, and both were wrong. In the sim the night's 40 cards still had 9 of 11 wrong ones stamped verified.
options.senior: A model grading answers, a model as judge, has habits of its own, and one of the commonest is favouring what it would have written. A generator grading a model trained on its own output shares its mistakes, so agreement measures likeness, not truth. Grade against answers checked by people or sources, and measure any model grader against a hand-checked set before you trust it.

options.text: Have Eirlys check every card by hand each night before we record.
options.verdict: Safe tonight, and the sheet still lies
options.part2: Eirlys went back to checking every card from Thursday: 40 cards an episode at about four and a half minutes each, 3 hours a night. In the sim, all 11 of the night's wrong cards are caught, and nothing wrong reached a contestant. But nothing else changed. The sheet still said 97%, the checker still agreed with her on only 72 of 100 practice cards, and Mr Thirlwell's next build was planned the same way, drawn from the same archive afterwards. When Eirlys took a week off in November, the stamps were all anyone had, and nobody knew what they were worth.
options.senior: A person checking everything is a sound safety net for a night or a season, and for a quiz the cost is three hours an episode. As a plan it leaves the measurement broken: the checker is never fixed, its score still lies, and the next build repeats the mistake. Keep the hand check while you rebuild the test honestly.

sim.title: Find the twins in Wakeful's test set
sim.lede: You're Mehwish on Monday 12 October, just before midnight. No real model runs here: every number is a count from given data. Given: 2,000 checked archive questions, rewritten by the bigger model 3 times each (6,000 pairs) or 10 times (20,000). The test set drawn from the archive afterwards has 200 cards in three groups: 164 with a twin at 3 or 10 rewrites, 24 with a twin only at 10, and 12 never; unseen, the checker would stamp 136, 20 and 10 of them right. A card with a twin in training is always stamped right. A test set written fresh and locked before generating has 6 cards the archive asked before (twins; unseen, 4 right) and 194 others (unseen, 140 right). The twin filter drops every pair that shares the answer and most words with a test card. The 100 practice cards on new topics: 72 agree with Eirlys, in every setting. The night's 40 cards: 11 wrong, 9 of them stamped verified. The 100-pair sample: 8 wrong. A hand check takes about 4.5 minutes a card. The bigger model, asked to grade the practice stamps, marks 91 right.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as released, 164 twins and 194 of 200 (97%). Check the night's 40 cards by hand: 9 of 11 wrong ones verified. Run the practice cards: 72, so the sheet overstates by 25 points. Switch on the sample: 8 of 100, about 480 of 6,000. Turn on the twin filter: 166 (83%). Then lock the test set first: 144 of 200 (72%), 0 points. Try 20,000 pairs with everything off: 99%. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the writers' room was haunted. The checker's 6,000 training pairs were made by a bigger model from the same archive the test set was later drawn from, so 164 of the 200 test cards had a reworded twin in training, and 97% measured what the checker remembered. On new topics it agrees with a checked answer 72 times in 100, and 8 in 100 of its made-up lessons were wrong.

steps.title: How the pairs were made, and what can go wrong.
steps.text: Data a model makes for training is synthetic data. Wakeful's went in three steps. First, the bigger model took each of the 2,000 checked archive questions. Second, it rewrote each three times in new words. Third, it gave each rewrite the right answer, stamped verified, or a wrong one, stamped check: 6,000 training pairs. What can go wrong at the third step: the model can change a fact while rewording and still stamp it verified. Mehwish's sample of 100 found 8, so roughly 480 of the 6,000 taught a wrong stamp. Wang and colleagues' Self-Instruct, which built a large set of instructions this way, reviewed a sample of 200 of its own and found the output correct in 58% of them. Made-up data needs reading, by a person, against a source.

steps.title: Why 97% measured memory.
steps.text: A test set works only if the model has never seen its items. Here the test was drawn from the same archive after every archive question had been rewritten into training, so the checker had in effect seen most of it. That overlap is contamination. The record shows it plainly: on the 164 test cards with a twin the checker scored 164 of 164; on the 36 without, 30, and those were still archive topics. Series 11 reused archive topics, so the stamps held all summer. Series 12 is new topics, and on 100 practice cards the checker agrees with Eirlys only 72 times. On the night's cards it stamped 9 of 11 wrong answers verified: on new topics, verified says little. Deng and colleagues describe the same gap in large models, between inflated benchmark scores and actual performance.

steps.title: The fix, in order.
steps.text: First, write the test set before generating anything: 200 cards on the topics that are coming, checked against sources, and locked where the data-making cannot reach. Second, generate the pairs. Third, run the twin filter: compare every pair with every test card and drop any that shares the answer and most of the words. Wakeful's archive repeats itself, and 6 locked cards had been asked before in nearly the same words. Fourth, check a random sample of the pairs against their sources, and fix or drop what is wrong. Then train, and score on the locked cards. In the sim that gives 144 of 200, 72%, the same as the practice cards. What can go wrong: the word rule misses a rewrite that changes most words but keeps the answer, and the locked cards stop being clean the moment anyone pastes one into a prompt.

steps.title: Why the other replies fail.
steps.text: Twenty thousand pairs from the same 2,000 questions raises the twins to 188 of 200 and the sheet to 99%, while the practice cards stay at 72 and the wrong pairs grow to about 1,600. Letting the bigger model grade the stamps gives 91 of 100 where Eirlys's sources give 72: a grader that wrote the training data shares its mistakes and favours answers like its own. Eirlys checking every card catches all 11, at 3 hours an episode, and leaves the sheet at 97% and the next build made the same way.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: the locked test set, 200 fresh cards written first; then the bigger model generates 6,000 pairs from the 2,000 archive questions; then the twin filter drops pairs that echo a test card, 6 found; then the sample check, 8 wrong in 100. Bottom row: training; then the score on the locked cards, 144 of 200, 72%; then the sheet, 72%, the same as the practice cards.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right. The test set is written and locked first, so the bigger model never rewrites it. The pairs are generated from the archive, the twin filter drops any pair that echoes a locked card, and a random sample is checked by hand. Only then is the checker trained, and it is scored on the locked cards: 144 of 200, 72%, the same as the practice cards, so the sheet is true before release.

fix.title: The fix: write and lock the test set first, filter out twins, check a sample of the made-up pairs
fix.text: Before any training data is generated, write the test set on the topics the checker will actually face, check every card against sources, and lock it where the generating step and the people running it cannot read it. Generate the pairs. Compare every pair with every test card and drop any that shares the answer and most of the words, because an archive repeats itself. Pick a random sample of the pairs, check each against its source, and fix or drop the wrong ones; if the error rate is high, compare every pair's answer with its source question before training. Train, then score on the locked cards and print that number on the sheet. Score every later build on the same locked cards, and never paste one into a prompt or a training file.

limits: The twin filter's word rule catches close rewrites only. A pair that changes most of the words but keeps the answer slips past, which is why locking the test set before generating matters more than the filter.

A sample of 100 gives a rough rate, not a list: 8 in 100 suggests about 480 wrong pairs in 6,000, but the true number could be some way either side, and only a full comparison with the sources finds every one.
An honest 72% does not make the checker better on new topics. It only tells you, before release, that the stamp needs a person behind it until better training data moves the locked score.

explain.seniorTake: Synthetic data is a fine way to get training examples quickly, and two things go wrong with it often enough to plan for. Its answers can be wrong, so read a random sample against a source before you train, and fix the generator or check every item if the rate is high. And it is easy to make it from the same pool you later test on, so the test quietly measures memory. Decide the test set first, on the cases you will actually face, and lock it away from the generating step, from training and from prompts. Then filter training examples that share the answer and most words with any test item, because real archives repeat themselves. Expect the honest score to be lower, and print that one. A high score on a test the model has in effect already seen tells you what it remembers, not what it can do, and a quiz show finds that out at 01:15 on the first night of new topics.

realWorld.title: Self-Instruct, 2022: filter what you generate
realWorld.text: Yizhong Wang and colleagues built training data by having a model write instructions for itself. Their abstract reads: Our pipeline generates instructions, input, and output samples from a language model, then filters invalid or similar ones before using them to finetune the original model. Their similarity rule reads: a new instruction is added to the task pool only when its ROUGE-L similarity with any existing instruction is less than 0.7. ROUGE-L is a score of how much wording two texts share.

realWorld.title: Self-Instruct's own quality check
realWorld.text: To check quality they write: we randomly sample 200 instructions and randomly select 1 instance per instruction. Their finding: most of the generated instructions are meaningful, while the generated instances may contain more noise. In their table, the output was a correct and acceptable response in 58% of the sample, and all fields were valid in 54%.

realWorld.title: Deng et al., 2023: inflated scores
realWorld.text: Chunyuan Deng and colleagues open: Recent observations have underscored a disparity between the inflated benchmark scores and the actual performance of LLMs, raising concerns about potential contamination of evaluation benchmarks. LLMs are large language models. In one test they hid an answer option and asked models to guess it: Further, in the MMLU benchmark, ChatGPT and GPT-4 demonstrated an exact match rate of 52% and 57%, respectively.

asked: How do you know your eval set is not in your training data?
What are the risks of synthetic training data?
Your fine-tuned model scores 97% on your test set and users say it is poor. Where do you look first?
interview.answer: I make it true by construction, then check. By construction: I write or pick the test set first, on the cases the model will really face, and lock it before any training data is generated, out of reach of the generating step, the training files and any prompt. Then I check: I compare every training example with every test item and drop any that shares the answer and most of the wording, because source data repeats itself, and I report how many I dropped. With synthetic data the two risks are wrong answers and overlap. Wrong answers: a generator can change a fact while rewording, so I hand-check a random sample against a source, estimate the error rate, and fix the generator or check everything if the rate is high. Overlap: data made from the same pool as the test produces twins, so the score measures memory. If a model scores 97% and users say it is poor, I look for twins between test and training first, then score it on fresh items written after the fact, and I expect a lower number. If the company is certified to ISO/IEC 42001 or working toward it, these are the data quality and verification-before-release controls an auditor will ask about.

atWork: Look for a team that generated training data from the same pool its test set came from, and reports a high score. It is a common pattern: someone uses a large model to rewrite support tickets, documents or past questions into training examples, then draws the test set from the same pile afterwards. The first sign is usually users saying the model is worse than its number. Ask three things of every fine-tune. Was the test set written or chosen before any training data was generated, and is it kept out of training files and prompts? Has every training example been compared with every test item, and how many were dropped as twins? And has anyone read a random sample of the generated examples against a source, with the error rate written down? On the Build Night, the Nightwatch copilot's X2 reuses this case: keep its 50 synthetic incidents apart from anything used for training or prompts. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, check the clause numbers against the standard's own text; ISMS.online's guide lists Annex A control A.7.4, quality of data for AI systems, and A.6.2.4, AI system verification and validation. A locked test set, a twin count and a sampled error rate recorded at each build are the kind of evidence those controls are likely to need, and they cost far less to keep from the first build than to rebuild at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team had a large model rewrite 10,000 old support tickets into 30,000 training examples, fine-tuned a small model on them, then picked 500 tickets from the same pile as its eval and reported 96%. Users say the model is much worse than that. What went wrong, and how would you measure it properly?

keyIdeas.idea: The eval tickets have reworded copies in the training data, so the score measures memory: contamination
Write or choose the test set first and lock it away before generating, then drop training examples that echo it
Hand-check a random sample of the generated examples against a source, because made-up answers can be wrong

recall.model: The eval was drawn from the same pile after the examples were made, so most eval tickets have a reworded copy in training: contamination, and the 96% measures memory. To measure properly, write or choose the test set first, from fresh tickets, and lock it away before generating anything; then drop any training example that shares the answer and most words with a test item, a near-duplicate. Also hand-check a sample of the generated examples against a source, since a model can write wrong answers, and note the error rate.

recall.prompt: Which number tells Mr Thirlwell most honestly how the checker will do on series 12?
options: 164 of 164 on cards with a twin
91 of 100 from the bigger model's grade
recall.why: The practice cards are on series 12's new topics, never rewritten into training and checked by Eirlys against sources. The 194 and the 164 are inflated by twins, and the 91 comes from a grader that shares the checker's mistakes.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: we score our fine-tuned model by asking the same large model that generated its training data whether each output is right. Agreement is 94%. Any problem?

keyIdeas.idea: The grader shares the generator's mistakes and favours answers like its own, so agreement measures likeness, not truth
Score against answers checked by people or sources, such as a golden set
Measure the grader itself against a hand-checked set before trusting it

recall.model: Yes. The grader made the training data, so it shares the model's mistakes and tends to pass answers like its own; 94% measures likeness, not truth. Score against answers checked by people or sources, such as a golden set. If you want a model grader for speed, measure the grader first: compare it with a hand-checked set and keep it only where it agrees with people.

recall.prompt: Mehwish's sample of 100 made-up pairs had 8 wrong. If the bigger model writes 20,000 pairs the same way, about how many would carry a wrong stamp?
recall.why: 8 in 100 is 8%, and 8% of 20,000 is 1,600. About 480 is 8% of the original 6,000. A sample gives a rate, so the count grows with the data.

recall.prompt: In Self-Instruct, as Wang and colleagues describe it, when is a newly generated instruction added to the task pool?
options: Only when a person has approved it
Only when its ROUGE-L similarity with any existing instruction is less than 0.7
Only when the model rates it above 0.7
recall.why: The paper reads: a new instruction is added to the task pool only when its ROUGE-L similarity with any existing instruction is less than 0.7. ROUGE-L scores shared wording, so near-copies are kept out.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. The locked test set worked: the January build scored 144 of 200 on it and the sheet said 72%. For the April build, a writer gave the bigger model 30 of the locked cards as examples of good cards to imitate when it made the new pairs. The April checker scores 168 of 200 on the locked cards, 84%. On 100 new practice cards it agrees with Eirlys on 74. Mr Thirlwell wants to print 84%.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is 84% real, and what should Wakeful do with the locked cards now?

Retire or replace the 30 exposed cards and score on the untouched ones, writing new locked cards
Make it a rule that locked cards never go into training files or prompts, and run the twin filter against prompts too

coldCase.model: No. The 30 cards leaked into the new pairs through the prompt, so the bigger model's rewrites of them are twins of locked cards: the set is contaminated again, and 84% is inflated. The 74 on new practice cards is the figure to print. Retire those 30, score on the other 170 until Eirlys and the writers write new locked cards to replace them, and make it a rule that locked cards never go into training files or prompts; run the twin filter against the generating prompt as well as the pairs.

sources.title: Yizhong Wang, Yeganeh Kordi, Swaroop Mishra, Alisa Liu, Noah A. Smith, Daniel Khashabi and Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions, arXiv 2212.10560 (2022), read 15 October 2026: Our pipeline generates instructions, input, and output samples from a language model, then filters invalid or similar ones before using them to finetune the original model; a new instruction is added to the task pool only when its ROUGE-L similarity with any existing instruction is less than 0.7; we randomly sample 200 instructions and randomly select 1 instance per instruction; most of the generated instructions are meaningful, while the generated instances may contain more noise; Table 2: output correct and acceptable 58%, all fields valid 54%

Chunyuan Deng, Yilun Zhao, Xiangru Tang, Mark Gerstein and Arman Cohan, Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models, arXiv 2311.09783 (submitted 16 November 2023), read 15 October 2026: Recent observations have underscored a disparity between the inflated benchmark scores and the actual performance of LLMs, raising concerns about potential contamination of evaluation benchmarks; Further, in the MMLU benchmark, ChatGPT and GPT-4 demonstrated an exact match rate of 52% and 57%, respectively
